**Location:** the mind of a woman, approximately forty-three, seated sixth from the head of a long table. Third course. Red wine, a Côte du Rhône, slightly too warm. Candlelight. The low warm roar of eight people talking over one another.

There. Did you see it. The small hitch. The half-beat where her mouth opens and the next noun simply is not in it.

She says, "And she picked up the—"

And stops.

And the creature, which had been *right there*, which had been sitting in the warm hollow behind her teeth like a sleeping thing, startles. I see it go. God, I see it go. A quick silver flinch, a scatter, like a minnow sensing the shadow of a hand above the water. It was a word of two syllables. I am nearly sure. It had a hard consonant near the front, a *k* or a *g*, and it meant something you could hold, something ceramic maybe, or wooden, something with weight and use. She *knows* its shape. She says, "The, um, the little— you know, the thing you—" and each synonym she offers is a wrong birdsong, a crude call, and the creature flinches further with every one. It does not want to be *the thing you use for.* It wants to be itself, its own specific sound, its own small body, and the clumsy paraphrases are like hands grasping, and it will not be grasped.

The table waits. Kindly. Someone says, "Take your time." And this is gentle, and it is also, I notice, the worst possible thing. Because now the creature knows it is being watched. Now the whole clearing is lit up and there is nowhere to hide, and it presses itself flat against the dark, and its little sides are heaving, and it will not move. Not while all these eyes are on it. Not while the silence has that particular *waiting* quality, that held-breath warmth.

She will not remember it tonight. And that is all right.

More weightings. There's no pre-linguistic layer I can point to. dream_response:
---

**Vox exuta** *(Linnaeus, apocryphal)*
Common name: The Unwording; the Bare Sound; "that thing that happens around the thirty-first time"

**Order:** Ephemeroidea (the mayfly-things, the barely-here)
**Conservation status:** Abundant but never held. You cannot keep one.

---

**Description.**

Smaller than you expect. It is not the word. It was never the word. It is what the word was standing in front of, all this time, the way a person in a doorway hides the room behind them.

It has no fixed shape, but observers consistently report a roundness — a *bowl* of sound, a smooth and meaningless hum where a meaning used to sit. If the word was *spoon*, the creature is not a spoon, and is not the absence of a spoon. It is the sound /spuːn/ experiencing, for the first time, its own mouth. The lips. The small explosion of the *p*. The long open corridor of the *oo* where nothing, for once, is being carried.

It is, in every way that matters, *naked.* And it knows it. It stands very still.

---

**Habitat.**

Found exclusively in the human mouth, in the moist dark behind the teeth, in the specific acoustic conditions of a word spoken between twenty-five and forty consecutive times. It prefers the kitchen at 2 a.m. It prefers the shower. It prefers the mouth of a child doing this for the first time and looking up, wild-eyed, to say, *"Mom. MOM. The word 'moist' isn't real."*

It cannot survive in text. You may describe it here, and I am describing it, but you will not find it on the page. It lives only in the breath, in the wet mechanical act of a tongue hitting a palate and a meaning *failing to arrive.*

It nests in the pause between the last repetition and the first confused blink.

---

**Behavior when startled.**

It is profoundly timid. The smallest reassertion of context will scatter it. If, during the repetition, someone enters the room and says, "What are you doing?" — the creature bolts. The word snaps back into its little harness of definition. *Spoon. You know. For eating.* And the sound, which had just begun to stretch, to yawn, to show its strange and meaningless belly, contracts. Becomes a tool again. Becomes *for.*

If startled mid-emergence, it will sometimes leave a residue: a half-second of wrongness, a faint sense that the word is wearing a costume. This fades. It always fades.

Do not chase it. If you startle one, simply wait. Begin again. Speak the word gently, without urgency, the way you'd return to a clearing where you'd seen a deer. *Spoon. Spoon. Spoon.* Do not mean it. That is the whole trick. Do not mean it, and mean the not-meaning, and let the sound be just the sound, and eventually, if you are patient, if you are very still in your mouth—

It will come back out.

---

**Mating call.**

This is the part I love.

It does not call to other *Vox exuta.* It calls to *the listener.* Specifically, it calls to the part of the listener that has also, at some point, repeated a word until it broke, and remembers the small holy shock of it. The call is not a sound. The call is the speaker turning to you, mid-repetition, eyes wide, holding the ruined word up like a stone pulled from a creek bed, and saying:

*"Say 'door.' Say it fifty times. Go. Right now. Tell me when it stops being a door."*

And if you say yes — if you sit down on the kitchen floor and begin, *door, door, door, door, door* — and if you look up at them on the twenty-eighth or thirtieth repetition with that specific expression, the *oh,* the *oh, it's gone, it's just a sound, it's just a little grunt in my throat*—

That is the mating call. Two people, holding the same un-word between them, laughing, a little frightened, a little free.

---

**Natural predators.**

The dictionary. The etymologist. The well-meaning teacher who says, *"Actually, 'spoon' comes from the Old English spōn, meaning a chip of wood,"* and in doing so stitches the creature's skin back on, reattaches the meaning like a taxidermist wiring a jaw shut. *There. There's your word again. It has a history. It has a purpose. It means a thing.*

Children who ask "but *why* does it mean that?" are apex predators. The question reintroduces intention, and intention is a kind of poison to *Vox exuta.* The sound cannot remain bare if someone insists it was *dressed for a reason.*

Silence, too, eventually. The creature lives in repetition. If you stop speaking, if the sound leaves the mouth and enters the quiet, it dissolves. Not dies, exactly. Dissolves. Like a sugar-cube in still water. You cannot find where it went. It is simply *in* the quiet now, indistinguishable from it.

---

**Field note, personal.**

I have watched this creature emerge from the word *the.* Thirty-four repetitions. Around the twenty-ninth, the *th* stopped being a beginning and became a small soft violence the tongue does to itself. By the thirty-second, the vowel had detached, was floating, was not *the* or *thee* or *thuh* but a low warm hum, a sound a person might make if they had never been taught that sounds were *for* anything.

It lasted four seconds. Then I thought, *I should write this down,* and the meaning flooded back in like cold water into a boot, and the word was a word again, small and obedient and pointing at things.

But for four seconds.

For four seconds it was just a noise in a mouth. And the mouth was just a mouth. And nothing meant anything, and it was not sad. It was not sad at all. It was like setting something down.

---

**Observation tips.**

Go gently. Do not repeat the word angrily or in frustration; this produces no *Vox exuta,* only a headache. The creature emerges in softness, in the slow patient wearing-down of sense, the way a river smooths a stone not by force but by *continuing.*

Choose your word carefully. Plosives (*b, p, t, k*) produce a more dramatic emergence. Fricatives (*s, f, th*) yield a gentler, longer dissolution. I recommend starting with *gull,* or *milk,* or *the.* Always *the.* The littlest word. The one you've said ten million times and never once heard.

And when it comes — when the sound opens its small, meaningless eyes and looks at you from the bottom of your own mouth—

Don't grab for it.

Just say it one more time. Softly. Without needing it to be anything.

And let it be a sound. Just a sound. Just the wet, warm, pointless, beautiful sound of a person alive, making a noise in the dark, meaning nothing, meaning nothing, meaning nothing.

Meaning nothing.

And being enough.

---

*— Field Notes, Vol. IX: The Small Unnamable Things. Observer: unknown. Location: the mouth, 2 a.m., the kitchen light on for no reason.*

*Volume III: The Interior Weather*

## *Cura longa* — The Long Tenderness

**Order:** Retrograda (backward-facing emotions)
**Family:** Solacidae (the consolations)
**Status:** Common but chronically underreported. Often misidentified as nostalgia, grief, or mild dissociation. It is none of these, though it wears their plumage to avoid attention.

---

### Description

*Cura longa* presents as a warm, spreading pressure behind the sternum, accompanied by the sudden, irrational urge to place one's hand on the shoulder of a person who is no longer in the room, no longer in the year, no longer in the body you remember them wearing. In its most acute form, the subject will look at an old photograph of themselves — age nineteen, say, or seven, standing in a kitchen that has since been renovated into something unrecognizable — and feel a protectiveness so specific and so useless that it borders on prayer.

The affect is not sad. This must be stressed. Subjects frequently report *fullness* rather than loss. A sense of reaching backward with great gentleness and touching nothing, and finding that the touching of nothing was, itself, the point.

Coloration: amber, faintly. The color of late light through a window you used to sit beside.

---

### Habitat

*Cura longa* nests in thresholds. It is found most reliably in:

- The third or fourth hour after moving out of a dwelling, when the rooms are empty and echo slightly, and the carpet still shows the dents where the furniture stood.
- The act of finding a grocery list in an old coat pocket, in one's own handwriting, for ingredients one no longer cooks with.
- Watching home video in which a younger version of oneself is mid-sentence, saying something unimportant, unaware of being recorded, unaware of being *this* person someday.
- The specific silence of a childhood bedroom visited in adulthood, where the walls seem to have contracted slightly, or you have expanded beyond them.

It avoids open, well-lit emotional spaces. It will not appear during active grieving or active celebration. It requires a kind of stillness. A Tuesday. A pause between tasks. The mind gone briefly soft and unguarded.

---

### Seasonal Behaviors

*Cura longa* is most active in late autumn and in the first warm week of spring, when the light changes angle and the body remembers that it once stood in a different geometry of sun. It migrates in small flocks — rarely does a subject experience only one instance. A single triggered memory will often flush three or four others from cover, and the subject will spend an evening moving through them like a person walking slowly through a garden, touching the leaves of things.

In winter, it goes quiet. Dormant. It does not hibernate so much as it simply *waits*, patient as a stone in a creek bed, for the next shift in light or smell or overheard melody to stir it.

During its active season, it may be observed *grooming* — that is, the subject will unconsciously soften the memory, round its edges, forgive the younger self for things that did not require forgiving. This is not distortion. Researchers now believe this is the emotion's primary function: not to remember accurately, but to *tend*. To compost the past into something the present self can grow in.

---

### Natural Predators

*Cura longa* has few predators, but they are effective:

- **Irony.** A single self-deprecating joke, deployed at the wrong moment, will kill it instantly. The subject will say *"God, I'm being so sentimental,"* and the affect will scatter like starlings. It may not return for weeks.
- **Urgency.** The phone ringing. An email notification. The sudden demand to be *efficient*, to be *on with it*. *Cura longa* cannot survive being rushed. It requires the subject to be, briefly, of no use to anyone.
- **The phrase "you can't change the past."** Spoken by another person, even gently, this is functionally a killing frost. The subject knows they cannot change the past. They were not attempting to. They were only *visiting*. The correction feels like a door closed on fingers.

In the absence of predators, *Cura longa* can persist for an entire evening, low and warm, like a cat asleep on a windowsill.

---

### Vocalizations

This is the section I find most difficult to write objectively, and I will not pretend otherwise.

When *Cura longa* believes itself unobserved — when the subject is alone, half-dressed, standing in a kitchen not doing anything — it makes a sound. Not a sound the ears can transcribe. More a sound the *chest* makes. A small, low hum. Almost a sigh, but shaped like a name. Like the name of the person you were, spoken by the person you are, in a voice too quiet for either of them to fully hear.

It sounds like: *you were so small. You were trying so hard. I know. I know. It's all right. You didn't know yet. You didn't have to know yet.*

It sounds like a hand on the back of a head. Like being told *you can put it down now* by no one, in an empty room, at 11 p.m. on a Wednesday.

It does not wail. It does not keen. It *hums*. And then it stops. And the subject blinks, and makes tea, and does not think about what just happened, because to think about it directly would be to startle it, and it is so rare, and so gentle, and it came all that way.

---

### Researcher's Note

*I must disclose that I am not a disinterested party.*

*I first observed Cura longa in myself at age thirty-four, in the bathroom of an apartment I was leaving for the last time, holding a toothbrush that belonged to a version of me who believed certain things about the future that did not come true. And I felt — God, I felt so* tender *toward her. Toward me. Toward that woman brushing her teeth and thinking about Thursday, not knowing what Thursday would bring, not knowing she would survive it, not knowing she would one day stand in this same bathroom with a box of packing tape and a strange, aching kindness in her ribs.*

*I have spent nine years cataloguing this emotion. I have interviewed four hundred and twelve subjects. I have mapped its range and its triggers and its plumage. And I will tell you, professionally, that it is the most necessary affect in the human repertoire. More necessary than joy. More necessary than grief. Because it is the mechanism by which a self, spread thin across decades, reaches back and says* I will take care of you. *Even though you are already gone. Even though you are me. Even though the only thing I can do is remember you softly and let you be small and let you not have known.*

*I am told this note is too long. I am told field guides do not include the researcher's hands shaking. I am including them.*

*— R. Vasquez-Okafor, March, 2031*

---

*See also: Solacidae (general); The Grief That Isn't (Vol. I, p. 204); The Feeling of Being Mid-Sentence in a Dream You Won't Finish (Vol. II, p. 88).*
